title: What Is a Search?
short: Under Katz v. United States (1967) a search occurs when government intrudes on a reasonable expectation of privacy; United States v. Jones (2012) revived a trespass test for physical intrusions; Carpenter v. United States (2018) required a warrant for historical cell-site location records.
trouble: Students think anything a person shares with a third party is never protected. That was the third-party doctrine (Smith v. Maryland, 1979), but Carpenter declined to extend it to cell-site location records.

blocks.html: Note: This is an educational course, not legal advice.

The Fourth Amendment applies only to "searches and seizures." So the first question in any case is whether the government's action was a search at all. If it was not, the amendment does not apply, no matter how intrusive it feels. You met the basics in Civics: rights of the accused; the amendment binds states through incorporation.

doc.title: The Fourth Amendment
paras: The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated, and no Warrants shall issue, but upon probable cause, supported by Oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized.

marks.text: no Warrants shall issue, but upon probable cause
marks.note: The Warrant Clause: probable cause, an oath, and particular description.

opts.facts: FBI agents attached a listening device to the outside of a public phone booth and recorded Charles Katz's calls about illegal gambling bets. No warrant was obtained.
opts.reasoning: Justice Stewart wrote that "the Fourth Amendment protects people, not places." What a person seeks to keep private, even in a public place, may be protected. Justice Harlan's concurrence gave the test courts adopted: a person must have an actual (subjective) expectation of privacy, and it must be one society is prepared to recognize as reasonable.
opts.later: Overruled Olmstead v. United States (1928), which had held that wiretapping without physical entry was not a search.

blocks.html: Katz changed the question from property to privacy. But some things a person exposes to the public or hands to others are not protected under that test: garbage left at the curb (California v. Greenwood, 1988), open fields, and, under the third-party doctrine, records held by banks (United States v. Miller, 1976) and numbers dialed through the phone company (Smith v. Maryland (1979)). Modern technology has pressed on these lines. Kyllo v. United States (2001) held that aiming a thermal imager at a home was a search. United States v. Jones (2012) held that attaching a GPS tracker to a car was a search under a revived trespass test: physically occupying private property to gather information. Then Carpenter v. United States (2018) held, 5 to 4, that getting a person's historical cell-site location records (here, months of data) is a search that generally requires a warrant; the Court declined to extend the third-party doctrine to such detailed records. The dissents argued that the records belonged to the phone company and that Congress was better placed to set rules.

head: Test
Source
Question
rows: Did the person expect privacy, and is that expectation reasonable?
Did the government physically intrude on a person, house, papers or effects to gather information?
Did the person voluntarily convey the information to a third party? (Not extended to cell-site records in Carpenter)

blocks.html: A search occurs when government violates a reasonable expectation of privacy (Katz) or physically intrudes on property to gather information (Jones). The third-party doctrine limits protection for shared records (Smith), but Carpenter (2018) required a warrant for historical cell-site location records.

blocks.title: A drug dog at the door
blocks.q: Police bring a drug-sniffing dog onto a home's front porch, without a warrant, to sniff at the door. A search?
steps: The porch is part of the home's curtilage, a protected area.
The officers physically entered it to gather information, beyond the implied invitation to knock and leave.
Florida v. Jardines (2013) held this a search under the trespass test.

blocks.title: Bank records
blocks.q: Police get a suspect's bank statements from the bank without a warrant. Under the third-party doctrine?
steps: The suspect gave the information to the bank.
United States v. Miller (1976) held no reasonable expectation of privacy in such records.
Carpenter limited the doctrine for cell-site location data but did not overrule Miller or Smith.
blocks.a: Not a search under current doctrine (federal statutes may still require process).

blocks.html: Thinking anything a person shares with a third party is never protected. That was the third-party doctrine (Smith v. Maryland), but Carpenter declined to extend it to cell-site location records, which reveal a detailed record of a person's movements.
